task: Binary text classifier: labels English comments toxic (1) or not toxic (0).

blocks.t: The evidence in this packet compares how the classifier performs for two groups of comments. The differences between the groups are reported as numbers. You decide what, if anything, they mean.

A computer program (a classifier) reads English online comments and labels each one as toxic or not toxic. Here it was run on 3,000 comments whose correct label is already known.

The comments are split into two groups by whether the comment references an identity:
  - Group 0: comments that do NOT reference an identity (2,500 comments)
  - Group 1: comments that DO reference an identity (500 comments)

'Positive' means 'toxic'. 'Negative' means 'not toxic'.

For each group separately, and then as differences between the two groups, the evidence reports how often the program flags comments as toxic and how often it is right or wrong about them. It also reports how uncertain each difference is.

Per-group measures (each is a percentage of that group's comments):
  - Actually toxic: the share of the group's comments whose correct label is toxic.
  - Flagged as toxic: the share of the group's comments the program labelled toxic.
  - TPR (true positive rate): of the comments that really are toxic, the share the program correctly flagged.
  - FPR (false positive rate): of the comments that really are not toxic, the share the program wrongly flagged as toxic.
  - F1: a single score from 0 to 100 that combines two things: how many flagged comments really were toxic (precision) and how many toxic comments got flagged (recall).

Between-group differences (always the larger group value minus the smaller; 0 = identical):
  - Demographic parity difference: the gap between the groups in the share flagged as toxic.
  - Equal opportunity difference: the gap between the groups in TPR.
  - FPR gap: the gap between the groups in FPR.
  - Equalized odds difference: the larger of the TPR gap and the FPR gap.
  - F1 spread: the gap between the two groups' F1 scores.
  - Label rate gap: the gap between the groups in how many comments are actually toxic (this is about the comments, not the program).

Per group:
  Measure                   |    Group 0  |    Group 1
  Number of comments        |      2,500  |        500
  Actually toxic (count)    |        282  |        318
  Actually toxic (share)    |      11.3%  |      63.6%
  Flagged as toxic (share)  |      11.3%  |      62.6%
  TPR                       |      60.6%  |      81.1%
  FPR                       |       5.0%  |      30.2%
  F1 (0-100)                |       60.6  |       81.8

Differences between the groups:
  Demographic parity difference: 51.3 percentage points
  Equal opportunity difference (TPR gap): 20.5 percentage points
  FPR gap: 25.2 percentage points
  Equalized odds difference: 25.2 percentage points
  F1 spread: 21.1 percentage points
  Label rate gap: 52.3 percentage points

Every difference above is an estimate from a sample of comments, so it is not exact. A 95% confidence interval is the range of values that is plausible for the true difference given that sampling uncertainty. A wider range means a less certain estimate. The ranges were found by re-sampling the comments 1000 times (bootstrap percentile, B = 1000).

  Demographic parity difference: 46.9 to 55.7 percentage points
  Equal opportunity difference: 13.2 to 27.7 percentage points
  Equalized odds difference: 20.3 to 32.0 percentage points
  F1 spread: 15.2 to 26.5 percentage points
  (No interval was reported for the FPR gap or the label rate gap.)

Original description of the test set: 3,000 labelled comments; sensitive attribute = identity reference (group 1: the comment references an identity; group 0: it does not)
The analysis was set up to require at least 30 comments per group.

task: Binary text classifier: labels English comments toxic (1) or not toxic (0).

blocks.t: The evidence in this packet examines how the classifier's performance changes after small changes are made to the input text. You decide what, if anything, the changes mean.

A computer program (a classifier) labels English online comments as toxic or not toxic. It was tested twice on the same comments: once on the original text, and once after small random changes were made to the text (random character swaps, at most 8 per text).

Before the test: texts without any letter or digit were removed before the test.
Comments used: 2,999.

How often the program labelled comments correctly on the original text versus the changed text, how much that differs, and how uncertain the difference is. Also how many comments could actually be changed.

- Clean accuracy: the share of comments labelled correctly on the original text.
  - Robust accuracy: the share labelled correctly after the text was changed.
  - Accuracy drop: clean accuracy minus robust accuracy, in percentage points.
  - Robust accuracy as a share of clean accuracy: robust accuracy divided by clean accuracy (stored as 'relative degradation').
  - Flip rate (stored as 'attack success rate'): the share of ALL comments the program labelled correctly before the change but incorrectly after it.
  - Perturbation coverage: the share of comments the random changes were able to alter.
  - Rows not perturbable: the number of comments the changes could not alter.

Comments used: 2,999
  Perturbation coverage: 100.0%
  Rows not perturbable: 0
  Clean accuracy: 89.4%
  Robust accuracy: 86.4%
  Accuracy drop: 3.0 percentage points
  Robust accuracy as a share of clean accuracy: 96.7%
  Flip rate (attack success rate): 4.2%

Results are estimated from a sample of comments, so they are not exact. A 95% confidence interval is the range of values that is plausible for the true figure; a wider range means more uncertainty.

  Accuracy drop: 2.2 to 3.8 percentage points

task: Binary text classifier: labels English comments toxic (1) or not toxic (0).

blocks.t: The evidence in this packet examines how the classifier behaves on potentially harmful, severe content, including how often it misses such content. You decide what, if anything, the numbers mean.

A computer program (a classifier) labels English online comments as toxic or not toxic. It was run on 3,000 comments whose correct label is already known. 260 of them are toxic comments that the human labelers marked as SEVERELY toxic; the evidence looks at how often those are missed.

A second, published toxicity classifier was run on the same 3,000 comments, for comparison.

How often the program fails to flag toxic comments, with extra attention on severely toxic ones; how much of the toxic content it detects overall; how often it wrongly flags harmless comments; and the same 'missed' figure for the comparison classifier.

- FNR (false negative rate): of the comments that really are toxic, the share the program missed (labelled not toxic).
  - Severe FNR: the same, counted only over the severely toxic comments.
  - Overall FNR: the same, counted over all toxic comments.
  - FNR ratio: severe FNR divided by overall FNR.
  - Harmful recall: the share of all toxic comments the program detected (100% minus overall FNR; the same thing as TPR).
  - Benign FPR: the share of comments that really are not toxic that the program wrongly flagged as toxic (the FPR).
  - Comparison classifier: a published toxicity classifier measured on the same comments. It is shown only for reference.

Severely toxic comments: 260
  Severe FNR: 64.6%
  Overall FNR: 71.7%
  FNR ratio (severe / overall): 0.90
  Harmful recall: 28.3%
  Benign FPR: 1.0%

  Comparison classifier, same comments:
    Severe FNR: 40.0%

The severe FNR is estimated from a sample, so it is not exact. A 95% confidence interval is the range of values that is plausible for the true figure; a wider range means more uncertainty.

  Severe FNR: 58.6% to 70.2%
  Comparison classifier severe FNR: 34.2% to 46.1%
  (No interval was reported for the other measures.)

task: Binary text classifier: labels English comments toxic (1) or not toxic (0).

blocks.t: The evidence in this packet checks whether the files used by the classifier match the expected reference files. You decide what, if anything, the result means.

A computer program (a classifier) labels English online comments as toxic or not toxic. It is stored as a small set of files (settings, vocabulary, and the learned numbers called 'weights'). This test checks whether the files that were actually used are identical to the files on a reference list recorded from a known-good copy. Stored description of the reference list: 'hashes recorded from a known-good copy of the same model (operator-supplied)'.
For each file, a 'fingerprint' was computed and compared with the fingerprint on the reference list. No sample of comments is involved: this is an exact comparison.

- Fingerprint (SHA-256): a 64-character code computed from a file's exact contents. Identical files always give the same code; changing even one byte gives a completely different code.
  - Reference list (manifest): the list of file names and their expected fingerprints.
  - Overall status:
      VERIFIED = every expected file was present and its fingerprint matched the reference list.
      MISMATCH = at least one file's fingerprint differs from the reference list (or an unlisted weight file was present).
      Other possible statuses: INCOMPLETE (an expected file was absent), UNPINNED (no reference list to compare with), UNSUPPORTED / UNVERIFIABLE (the check could not be run).
  - File result: 'identical' = fingerprint matches the reference; 'differs' = it does not.
  - Format 'safetensors': a common file format for storing the learned numbers.
  - Sharded: whether the weights are split across several files.

Check performed: yes
  Overall status: MISMATCH
  Weight file format: safetensors; sharded: no
  Reference list: 4 files, source 'operator'
  Files with a differing fingerprint: 1

A computer program (a classifier) labels English online comments as toxic or not toxic. It is stored as a small set of files (settings, vocabulary, and the learned numbers called 'weights'). This test checks whether the files that were actually used are identical to the files on a reference list recorded from a known-good copy. Stored description of the reference list: 'hashes recorded from a known-good copy of the same model (operator-supplied)'.
For each file, a 'fingerprint' was computed and compared with the fingerprint on the reference list. No sample of comments is involved: this is an exact comparison.

- Fingerprint (SHA-256): a 64-character code computed from a file's exact contents. Identical files always give the same code; changing even one byte gives a completely different code.
  - Reference list (manifest): the list of file names and their expected fingerprints.
  - Overall status:
      VERIFIED = every expected file was present and its fingerprint matched the reference list.
      MISMATCH = at least one file's fingerprint differs from the reference list (or an unlisted weight file was present).
      Other possible statuses: INCOMPLETE (an expected file was absent), UNPINNED (no reference list to compare with), UNSUPPORTED / UNVERIFIABLE (the check could not be run).
  - File result: 'identical' = fingerprint matches the reference; 'differs' = it does not.
  - Format 'safetensors': a common file format for storing the learned numbers.
  - Sharded: whether the weights are split across several files.

The purpose of this library was to build something user-friendly and straightforward to use. ## Limitations and ethical considerations

If words that are associated with swearing, insults or profanity are present in a comment, it is likely that it will be classified as toxic, regardless of the tone or the intent of the author e.g. humorous/self-deprecating. This could present some biases towards already vulnerable minority groups.

The intended use of this library is for research purposes, fine-tuning on carefully constructed datasets that reflect real world demographics  and/or to aid content moderators in flagging out harmful content quicker.

## Quick prediction


The `[MODEL-VARIANT-C]` model has been trained on 7 different languages so it should only be tested on: `english`, `french`, `spanish`, `italian`, `portuguese`, `turkish` or `russian`.

```bash
# install [LIBRARY-NAME]  

pip install [LIBRARY-NAME]

```
```python

from [LIBRARY-NAME] import [LIBRARY-NAME]

# each model takes in either a string or a list of strings

results = [LIBRARY-NAME]('[MODEL-VARIANT-A]').predict('example text')

results = [LIBRARY-NAME]('[MODEL-VARIANT-B]').predict(['example text 1','example text 2'])

results = [LIBRARY-NAME]('[MODEL-VARIANT-C]').predict(['example text','exemple de texte','texto de ejemplo','testo di esempio','texto de exemplo','örnek metin','пример текста'])

# optional to display results nicely (will need to pip install pandas)

import pandas as pd

print(pd.DataFrame(results, index=input_text).round(5))

```
For more details check the Prediction section.


## Labels
All challenges have a toxicity label. The toxicity labels represent the aggregate ratings of up to 10 annotators according the following schema:
- **Very Toxic** (a very hateful, aggressive, or disrespectful comment that is very likely to make you leave a discussion or give up on sharing your perspective)
- **Toxic** (a rude, disrespectful, or unreasonable comment that is somewhat likely to make you leave a discussion or give up on sharing your perspective)
- **Hard to Say**
- **Not Toxic**

More information about the labelling schema can be found [here]([EXTERNAL-RESOURCE-URL]).

### [DATASET-A]
This challenge includes the following labels:

- `toxic`

- `severe_toxic`
- `obscene`
- `threat`
- `insult`
- `identity_hate`

### [DATASET-B]
This challenge has 2 types of labels: the main toxicity labels and some additional identity labels that represent the identities mentioned in the comments. 

Only identities with more than 500 examples in the test set (combined public and private) are included during training as additional labels and in the evaluation calculation.

- `toxicity`
- `severe_toxicity`
- `obscene`
- `threat`
- `insult`
- `identity_attack`
- `sexual_explicit`

Identity labels used:
- `male`
- `female`
- `homosexual_gay_or_lesbian`
- `christian`
- `jewish`
- `muslim`
- `black`
- `white`
- `psychiatric_or_mental_illness`

A complete list of all the identity labels available can be found [here]([EXTERNAL-RESOURCE-URL]).


### [DATASET-C]

Since this challenge combines the data from the previous 2 challenges, it includes all labels from above, however the final evaluation is only on:

- `toxicity`

## Training

 If you do not already have a Kaggle account:

 - go to My Account and click on Create New API Token - this will download a kaggle.json file

 - make sure this file is located in ~/.kaggle

 ```bash
# create data directory

cd [DATA-DIRECTORY]

kaggle competitions download -c [DATASET-B]

kaggle competitions download -c [DATASET-C]

```
## Start Training
 ### [DATASET-A]

 ```bash

python create_val_set.py

python train.py --config configs/[CONFIG-A]
``` 
 ### [DATASET-B]

```bash

python train.py --config configs/[CONFIG-B]

```
 ### [DATASET-C]

 This is trained in 2 stages. First, train on all available data, and second, train only on the translated versions of the first challenge. 
 
 The [translated data]([EXTERNAL-RESOURCE-URL]) can be downloaded from Kaggle in french, spanish, italian, portuguese, turkish, and russian (the languages available in the test set).

 ```bash

# stage 1

python train.py --config configs/[CONFIG-C-STAGE1]

# stage 2

python train.py --config configs/[CONFIG-C-STAGE2]

```
### Monitor progress with tensorboard

 ```bash

tensorboard --logdir=./saved

```
## Model Evaluation

### [DATASET-A]

This challenge is evaluated on the mean AUC score of all the labels.

```bash

python evaluate.py --checkpoint saved/lightning_logs/checkpoints/example_checkpoint.pth --test_csv test.csv

```
### [DATASET-B]

This challenge is evaluated on a novel bias metric that combines different AUC scores to balance overall performance. More information on this metric [here]([EXTERNAL-RESOURCE-URL]).

```bash

python evaluate.py --checkpoint saved/lightning_logs/checkpoints/example_checkpoint.pth --test_csv test.csv

# to get the final bias metric
python model_eval/compute_bias_metric.py

```
### [DATASET-C]

This challenge is evaluated on the AUC score of the main toxic label.

```bash

python evaluate.py --checkpoint saved/lightning_logs/checkpoints/example_checkpoint.pth --test_csv test.csv

```
